name: Race Conditions and Atomicity
intent: Understand why code that is correct for one thread can give wrong answers when two threads run it at once, and which tools (locks, atomic operations, compare-and-swap) make a read-modify-write step safe.
scenario: Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter that starts at 0, so the answer should be 2. In a second case two customers each withdraw 80 from an account holding 100, so exactly one should succeed and 20 should be left. A deterministic scheduler tries every possible order of the threads' steps.
problem: A line such as counter++ looks like one action, but it is three: read the value, add one, write it back. If a second thread reads between the first thread's read and write, both write the same number and one update vanishes. The same shape hides in check-then-act code (check the balance, then withdraw). The bug appears only in some orders, so tests pass hundreds of times and production fails once a week.

howItWorks.title: Find the read-modify-write
howItWorks.text: A race condition needs shared data and a step that reads it, decides something from what it read, and writes back. In between, the thread holds a private copy that can go stale. counter++, balance -= x after if (balance >= x), and put-if-absent on a map are all this shape. Code that only reads shared data, or only touches data that one thread owns, has no race.

howItWorks.title: Interleavings decide the result
howItWorks.text: The scheduler may switch threads between any two steps, and the program does not control when. Two threads with 4 steps each have 70 possible orders (8 choose 4; the simulation's 2 threads x 2 increments, each increment a read then an add-and-write), and for the unsafe counter most of them are wrong. The wrong ones are not rare accidents: whenever both threads read before either writes, the second write overwrites the first (a lost update).

howItWorks.title: Make the whole step indivisible with a lock
howItWorks.text: A lock lets one thread at a time into the critical section, so the read, the check and the write cannot be mixed with another thread's. The lock must cover the whole read-modify-write. Locking the read and the write separately releases the lock in between, which is exactly the gap the bug lives in, so the unsafe orders are all still possible.

howItWorks.title: Or make the step a single atomic operation
howItWorks.text: Hardware and runtimes offer operations that read and update in one indivisible step: an atomic add (Interlocked.Increment in C#, AtomicInteger in Java, atomic counters in most languages). No other thread can see the value half-way, and there is no lock to wait for. It only works when the whole change fits one operation on one value.

howItWorks.title: Compare-and-swap for everything else
howItWorks.text: Compare-and-swap (CAS) says: set the value to new only if it still equals old, and tell me whether it worked. A thread reads, computes, and tries to swap; if another thread got in first, the swap fails and the thread re-reads and tries again. No thread blocks, and no update is lost, but the code must be safe to run more than once, because a failed attempt repeats its computation.

pros: A lock around the whole read-modify-write is simple and correct for any change, however large
An atomic operation is lock-free for simple updates, so nothing can wait or deadlock on it
A compare-and-swap loop makes any single-value update safe without blocking other threads
Seeing every interleaving, not one lucky run, is what turns a rare bug into a countable one
cons: A lock makes threads wait, and a thread that holds it while it is paused stalls the rest
An atomic operation protects one value, not a rule that spans two values (a balance and a log)
A CAS loop can retry many times when many threads fight over one value, and repeats its computation each time
None of these show up in a normal test: the failing interleaving may be one in millions
whenToUse: A lock when the critical section updates several values that must change together
An atomic operation for counters, flags and sequence numbers shared between threads
CAS or a version number when conflicts are rare and holding a lock would be a bigger cost than a retry
whenNotToUse: Locks or atomics around data that only one thread ever touches: it adds cost and no safety
A CAS loop whose body has side effects (sending an email, charging a card) that a retry would repeat
Hand-built atomics for a rule that spans several values: use a lock or a transaction instead
pitfalls: Believing counter++ is atomic because it is one line: on a plain variable it is a read, an add and a write in any mainstream language (only a type declared atomic, such as C++ std::atomic, makes it one step), and Python's global interpreter lock does not change that for compound steps
Locking the read and the write separately: the lock is released between them, so the lost update still happens
Check-then-act on a shared structure (if not in map, then add) without holding one lock across both
Making two values atomic one by one when the rule links them: each update is safe, the pair is not
Trusting a test that passed: a race fails only in some orders, so a green run proves little
Assuming a single-threaded runtime has no races: in JavaScript the same bug appears across an await, because other tasks run while you wait

roles.label: Thread A
roles.description: Runs counter++ as three steps: read, add, write.

roles.label: Thread B
roles.description: Runs the same code at the same time on the same counter.

roles.label: Shared counter
roles.description: The one value both threads read and write.

roles.label: Scheduler
roles.description: Decides which thread runs next, and may switch between any two steps.

roles.label: Lock
roles.description: Lets one thread at a time through a protected section.

quiz.question: Two threads each run counter++ ten thousand times on a shared counter that starts at 0. The final value is below 20,000 and differs from run to run. Why?
options: Each thread's updates are cached privately, and the counter only counts the last thread to finish.
The runtime drops increments whenever two threads are running on different processor cores.
An increment is a read, an add and a write, and a thread paused in between has its update overwritten.
Integer counters hold at most 10,000 values, so the extra increments are discarded.
quiz.explanation: counter++ is three steps, and the scheduler can switch threads between them. If both threads read the same value before either writes, both write the same result and one increment is lost. How many are lost depends on the interleaving, which changes from run to run.

quiz.question: A developer takes a lock to read the balance, releases it, checks the balance, then takes the lock again to subtract. Two customers still both succeed in withdrawing 80 from 100. Why?
options: The lock is released between the read and the write, so another thread can change the balance after the check.
A lock only protects against reads, never against writes, so the subtraction was unprotected.
Locks are ignored by the second thread unless both threads use the same variable name.
The balance is stored in two places, and the lock only covers one of the copies.
quiz.explanation: The lock has to cover the whole read-check-write. With two separate critical sections, both customers can read 100 and pass the check before either subtracts, and the balance ends at -60. One lock held across all three steps leaves only two possible orders.

quiz.question: A compare-and-swap on a shared value fails because another thread changed it first. What should the thread do?
options: Write its result anyway, since its computation was correct when it started.
Give up and report an error, because the failed swap shows the data is corrupt.
Wait for the other thread to finish, then continue from the stale value it already holds.
Re-read the current value, redo its computation from that value, and try the swap again.
quiz.explanation: A failed swap means the value it based its work on is stale. Writing anyway is the lost update again. The thread must re-read, recompute and retry, which is why the code inside a CAS loop must be safe to run more than once.
